title: Why Aramex Started by Delivering Other Couriers' Parcels
dek: In 1982 a young car-rental clerk and a family friend set out to build a Middle Eastern courier, and found their way in by working for the giants.

story.event: Starting an express courier company in Amman by delivering for American couriers
story.summary: In 1982 Fadi Ghandour, a recent political science graduate working at a car-rental firm in Jordan, and family friend Bill Kingson founded Aramex with offices in Amman and New York to build a courier for the Middle East. Facing postal monopolies, little capital and regional war, they partnered with local agents and chose a 'wholesale' niche, delivering Middle East parcels for FedEx, Airborne Express and others on their paperwork. Airborne declined to buy half the company for $100,000 in 1984 but became a client; Aramex listed on NASDAQ in 1997.
paragraphs: In the early 1980s Fadi Ghandour, in his early twenties, was in Jordan with a political science degree from George Washington University and a job at a car-rental company, "literally renting cars," as he later put it. He had interviewed at the central bank and decided against it. Then a family friend, Bill Kingson, who ran a very small courier business in the north-eastern United States and flew cancelled cheques for banks there, put an idea to him: FedEx, UPS and DHL were building a new industry, and the Middle East had few competitors in it.

Ghandour calls himself an accidental entrepreneur. He had used FedEx as a student and thought the region's postal services a disaster; with nothing to lose, he said, the two set out to build "a FedEx of the region." Aramex was founded in 1982, with offices in Amman and New York. Then the obstacles appeared. Postal authorities guarded their monopolies, and Jordan's licence took about six months. Money came from family and friends, two backers who left within a year or so, and a bank loan secured by a personal guarantee. That year, as Ghandour recalls, Israel invaded Lebanon, Iran and Iraq were at war and the oil price had fallen.

So they chose not to build much. In each city they partnered with existing messenger services and small cargo agents glad to earn a little extra for a delivery. And instead of fighting DHL for local customers, they offered American couriers with no Middle East network a deal: hand over your packages in New York and Aramex will deliver them on your own paperwork. The plan, Ghandour said, was to "deliver packages for the big boys and learn from them." In 1984 he and Kingson tried to sell half the company to Airborne Express for $100,000. Airborne declined, but became a client.

That niche carried Aramex for about ten years; in 1987 FedEx gave it all its business for the region. Aramex still opened offices of its own, one in London beside Airborne's. In 1996 Airborne paid $2 million for about nine per cent, and in 1997 Aramex became the first Arab-based company listed on NASDAQ. When DHL bought Airborne in 2003, Aramex had its own network and tracking system ready.

quote.text: To keep the proportion of things and give place to others without losing one's own position was the secret of success in the mundane drama.
quote.source_title: The Book of Tea, Project Gutenberg eBook #769
quote.connection: For about ten years Aramex delivered under other companies' names. Okakura, describing Taoist thought, treats that kind of giving place as a skill, but only if you keep your own position. Ghandour kept his by building offices and systems of his own, which is why losing Airborne did not sink him.

reflection: Being the small partner of a large organisation can feel like a lesser kind of work: their name on the paperwork, their standards, their deadlines. Ghandour treated it as paid tuition. FedEx and Airborne, he said, forced Aramex to learn, because it had to meet their standards on every delivery.

The other half of his story is less visible. While Aramex served them, it kept building something that was its own. If you are working inside someone else's system at the moment, a job, a partnership, a hospital's rules, it is worth knowing which part of what you are learning would still be yours if the arrangement ended.
invitation: Write down one thing you have learned this year from an organisation bigger than yours that you could carry anywhere. Keep the note where you will see it next month.

research_notes: The main source is Ghandour's 2017 Harvard Business School oral history; the transcript is the PDF linked from the HBS page. The $100,000 offer: in the oral history Ghandour hedges ('$100,000, I think ... I don't remember. Something around $100,000 for 50 percent'), while his own HBR article (2011) states the figure and the 1984 date plainly; the story uses the HBR version. In the oral history the interviewer frames the offer as 'by the mid-'80s' and Ghandour says 'even earlier'; HBR's 1984 is used. Kingson: the oral history says he flew aircraft 'for regional central banks in the US, carrying canceled checks' and had a very small courier business in the north-east; Wikipedia calls him a friend of Ghandour's father; the story calls him a family friend, as Ghandour does. Funding: the slate's 'bootstrapped' is kept, since there was no venture money, but the 500 Startups interview says early money came from family and friends, two other funders who left after about a year, and a bank loan secured by a personal guarantee; the story says so. FedEx: the 500 interview says FedEx gave Aramex all its regional business in 1987 (Wikipedia agrees on 1987); the oral history says FedEx later left on 30 days' notice after about ten years once it could get licences; that later exit is not in the story. The regional context (Israeli invasion of Lebanon in 1982, the Iran-Iraq war, the oil price) is Ghandour's recollection and is attributed to him. Headcount and revenue figures differ by date (8,100 staff in Tharawat 2010, about 13,800 in the SQLI interview, over 16,000 on Aramex's site today), so the story gives none. The William Davidson Institute case cited by Wikipedia is only available as an archived PDF the checker cannot read, so it is not cited; its IPO figures (US$24 million valuation, US$7 million raised) are not used. The Okakura passage describes Taoist ideas of conduct and is applied by analogy; Okakura wrote in English, so no translator is given.
